## Fundamentals of Causal Representation  
To represent causal relationships mathematically, researchers typically use Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). In these graphs, nodes represent variables, and directed edges (arrows) represent direct causal influences. A key framework for this is the Structural Causal Model (SCM). An SCM describes each variable as a function of its direct causes (parents) and an independent noise term :  
The noise term represents unobserved factors that influence but are independent of the other variables in the system. Causal Discovery with Continuous Additive Noise Models
Abstract
We consider the problem of learning causal directed acyclic graphs from an observational joint distribution. One can use these graphs to predict the outcome of interventional experiments, from which data are often not available. We show that if the observational distribution follows a structural equation model with an additive noise structure, the directed acyclic graph becomes identifiable from the distribution under mild conditions. This constitutes an interesting alternative to traditional methods that assume faithfulness and identify the Markov equivalence class of the graph, i.e., leaving some edges undirected. We provide practical algorithms for finitely many samples and provide an empirical evaluation.
1 Introduction
We consider a -dimensional random vector  with a joint distribution  and assume that there is a true acyclic causal graph  that describes the data generating process (see Section 1.3).
In this work we address the following problem of causal inference: given the distribution 
we try to infer the graph .
A priori, the causal graph contains information about the physical process that cannot be found in properties of the joint distribution.
One therefore requires assumptions connecting these two worlds. While traditional methods like PC, FCI or score-based approaches (see Section 2) make assumptions that enable us to recover the graph up to the Markov equivalence class, we investigate a different set of assumptions. If the data have been generated by an additive noise model, we will generically be able to recover the correct graph from the joint distribution.

Bayesian inference of causal effects from observational data in Gaussian graphical models
Abstract
We assume that multivariate observational data are generated from a distribution whose conditional independencies are encoded in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). For any given DAG, the causal effect of a variable onto another one can be evaluated through intervention calculus. A DAG is typically not identifiable from observational data alone. However, its Markov equivalence class (a collection of DAGs) can be estimated from the data. As a consequence, for the same intervention a set of causal effects, one for each DAG in the equivalence class, can be evaluated. In this paper, we propose a fully Bayesian methodology to make inference on the causal effects of any intervention in the system. Main features of our method are: (a) both uncertainty on the equivalence class and the causal effects are jointly modeled; (b) priors on the parameters of the modified Cholesky decomposition of the precision matrices across all DAG models are constructively assigned starting from a unique prior on the complete (unrestricted) DAG; (c) an efficient algorithm to sample from the posterior distribution on graph space is adopted; (d) an objective Bayes approach, requiring virtually no user specification, is used throughout. We demonstrate the merits of our methodology in simulation studies, wherein comparisons with current state-of-the-art procedures turn out to be highly satisfactory. Finally we examine a real data set of gene expressions for Arabidopsis thaliana.

octen.snippet:
This work addresses the following question: Under what assumptions on the
data generating process can one infer the causal graph from the joint
distribution? The approach taken by conditional independence-based causal
discovery methods is based on two assumptions: the Markov condition and
faithfulness. It has been shown that under these assumptions the causal graph
can be identified up to Markov equivalence (some arrows remain undirected)
using methods like the PC algorithm. In this work we propose an alternative by
defining Identifiable Functional Model Classes (IFMOCs). As our main theorem we
prove that if the data generating process belongs to an IFMOC, one can identify
the complete causal graph. To the best of our knowledge this is the first
identifiability result of this kind that is not limited to linear functional
relationships. We discuss how the IFMOC assumption and the Markov and
faithfulness assumptions relate to each other and explain why we believe that
the IFMOC assumption can be tested more easily on given data. We further
provide a practical algorithm that recovers the causal graph from finitely many
data; experiments on simulated data support the theoretical findings. cs.LG, stat.ML J. Peters, J. Mooij, D. Janzing, B. Schölkopf

A prediction model tells you P(Y∣X)P(Y \mid X): given observed features, what outcome is likely. A causal model tells you P(Y∣do(X))P(Y \mid do(X)): if you intervene to set XX to a particular value, what happens to YY. These are different quantities. Knowing that umbrellas correlate with rain does not mean distributing umbrellas will cause rain.

Pearl's framework provides the formal machinery for distinguishing association from causation. ## The PC (Peter-Clark) algorithm: constraint-based search for causal DAGs

The PC algorithm, named after its developers Peter Spirtes and Clark Glymour with significant contributions from Richard Scheines, stands as a foundational constraint-based method for recovering causal directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) from observational data. Introduced as an efficient refinement of earlier search procedures in the early 1990s, the algorithm operates in two primary phases to construct a causal structure that is consistent with the observed probability distribution. It begins by forming a complete undirected graph over the set of variables and systematically removes edges by testing for conditional independence, progressively increasing the size of conditioning sets until no further removals are justified. Once the undirected skeleton is obtained, the second phase orients edges by identifying unshielded colliders, or v-structures, where two variables are independent conditional on a third but dependent when conditioning on subsets that exclude it, and then applies a set of orientation rules to propagate directions while avoiding cycles. This process yields a pattern representing the Markov equivalence class of DAGs compatible with the data, capturing all causal features that are identifiable under the assumptions without enumerating every possible graph. By relying solely on conditional independence constraints rather than exhaustive enumeration or parametric scoring, the PC algorithm achieves polynomial time complexity in the number of variables for sparse graphs, making it computationally feasible for moderately high-dimensional problems where traditional exhaustive searches would be intractable. We study the problem of learning directed acyclic graphs from observational data in nonlinear models and provide finite-sample, nonasymptotic statistical guarantees in these models. Although widely studied, statistical guarantees for gradient-based methods in nonlinear models are missing from the literature. Under a generalized linear model for each node, we analyze a global nonsmooth objective combining an exact acyclicity constraint with a quasi-minimax concave penalty, which can be optimized via standard gradient-based solvers. We establish finite-sample guarantees under this model, including the most widely used logistic and Poisson models. Experiments corroborate structure recovery accuracy and computational performance, including both standardized data and negative controls as baselines.

Learning a directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a fundamental task that enables the discovery of underlying causal mechanisms (Schölkopf et al., 2021), which can help explain unknown phenomena (Dominici et al., 2025), aid in prediction accuracy, and boost out-of-distribution performance in downstream tasks (Lv et al., 2022; Saengkyongam et al., 2023; Kong et al., 2024).

We study differentiable causal structure learning for DAGs with GLM conditional distributions, allowing nonlinear relationships. To this aim, we first cast causal structure learning as an estimation problem with a single global objective over all topological orders, where the objective is defined for a broad class of generalized linear models (GLMs) over a class of continuous DAG coefficient matrices.

Causal relationships are often represented by directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where nodes correspond to variables and directed edges indicate cause-effect links (Pearl, [2009](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.21658v2#bib.bib33); Spirtes et al., [2000](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.21658v2#bib.bib42); Peters et al., [2017](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.21658v2#bib.bib36)).

webiq.title: Markov Equivalence Class in Causal Models
webiq.snippet:
A Markov Equivalence Class (MEC) is the set of all Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) that encode identical conditional-independence structures via d-separation. In observational or partially specified causal inference, a data-generating DAG cannot usually be determined uniquely from observational data; instead, only the implied MEC—i.e., the set of DAGs Markov-equivalent to the true structure—can be recovered. Each MEC can be represented by a unique completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG), in which compelled (invariant) edge orientations appear as directed edges and ambiguously oriented edges remain undirected.
